paper.title: OceanFlow: Coherent Flow Matching for Probabilistic Ocean Modeling
paper.abstract: Abstract Probabilistic ocean modeling is essential for risk-aware marine operations, climate analysis, and scientific decision-making, where downstream decisions depend on the conditional distribution of future ocean states rather than a single deterministic trajectory. Recent data-driven ocean models have made deterministic global ocean modeling increasingly accurate and efficient, but probabilistic ocean modeling remains underdeveloped. Specifically, perturbation-driven ensembles can create spread without explicitly optimizing the joint distribution of their members, often yielding poor calibration and physical inconsistency. To address these issues, we propose OceanFlow , a coherent flow matching framework for probabilistic global ocean modeling. OceanFlow first establishes a sharp, stable mean anchor for the conditional ensemble. Flow matching then learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law that jointly reshapes the residual distribution around this anchor at each transition, preserving the predictive center while refining state-dependent uncertainty. We further introduce a Factorized Dynamics Operator (FDO), which combines factorized transitions with a learned state-conditioned response to parameterize the mean anchor and residual-flow velocity. Extensive experiments show that OceanFlow improves ensemble-mean accuracy, probabilistic reliability, and physical-consistency diagnostics over competitive baselines, supporting coherent flow matching as an effective route toward data-driven probabilistic ocean modeling. Code is available at https://github.com/YuanGao-YG/OceanFlow .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Ocean modeling is essential for risk-aware marine operations, climate analysis, and scientific decision-making ( Kalnay, 2003 ; Lellouche et al., 2018 ; Tan et al., 2025b ) . Incomplete observations leave uncertainty in the initial ocean state, while nonlinear dynamics can amplify small state errors into substantially different future evolutions ( Lorenz, 2017 ; Leith, 1974 ) . Even an accurate deterministic estimate cannot characterize the range of plausible outcomes or their relative likelihoods. Probabilistic modeling can address this limitation by representing the conditional distribution of future ocean states, providing uncertainty information beyond a single trajectory. Recent data-driven models, including AI-GOMS ( Xiong et al., 2023 ) , XiHe ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , LangYa ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , and WenHai ( Cui et al., 2025 ) , have substantially advanced deterministic global ocean modeling, combining competitive predictive accuracy with considerably faster inference than traditional numerical models. These gains make ocean modeling more affordable and provide a strong foundation for efficient ensemble generation. However, despite this progress in deterministic modeling, data-driven probabilistic ocean modeling remains comparatively underexplored. Similar to initial-condition perturbation in numerical ensemble forecasting, data-driven ocean models can be extended to probabilistic modeling by perturbing their initial states and evolving the resulting members with a pretrained deterministic model ( Hao et al., 2025 ) . Prescribed perturbations can generate ensemble spread and improve ensemble-mean accuracy through averaging. However, members evolve independently without joint distributional optimization, potentially yielding distributions that deviate from physically plausible ocean variability and fail to faithfully represent uncertainty in the underlying dynamics. FuXi-ONS ( Huang et al., 2026 ) advances beyond prescribed noise by learning state-dependent, spatially structured perturbations for autoregressive ocean prediction. This provides a more adaptive representation of ensemble variability. Nevertheless, its memberwise prediction objective leaves ensemble calibration implicit, while member updates do not explicitly account for the evolving ensemble context. These advances motivate a central question: how can the ensemble be jointly refined to more faithfully characterize uncertainty in the underlying ocean dynamics while maintaining a controlled predictive center? Figure 1: Learning coherent ensemble laws for ocean modeling. (a) Deterministic modeling produces a single trajectory. (b) OceanFlow represents ocean uncertainty through a mean-anchored ensemble, jointly refining member residuals under a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law at each transition. To answer this question, we propose OceanFlow , a coherent flow matching framework for probabilistic ocean modeling. As illustrated in Figure 1 , OceanFlow learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law for the residual ensemble around a controlled mean anchor at each transition. This law couples member-specific transport paths through a shared velocity field conditioned on the ocean state and evolving ensemble context. Ensemble diversity is thus jointly refined as a conditional residual distribution, with final recentering preserving the predictive center. We further introduce a Factorized Dynamics Operator (FDO) that parameterizes both the mean anchor and residual-flow velocity through a unified composition of factorized dynamics and learned state-conditioned response. Our contributions can be summarized as: • We propose OceanFlow , a coherent flow matching framework for probabilistic ocean modeling that learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law around the mean anchor center. By coupling member residuals through the evolving ensemble context, it jointly refines the conditional distribution while preserving a controlled mean anchor. • We introduce a Factorized Dynamics Operator (FDO), which unifies factorized dynamics and a learned state-conditioned response within a single conditional operator formulation. FDO supports both an accurate deterministic reference for the mean anchor and a structured velocity field for residual transport. • Extensive experiments on global ocean simulation and forecasting tasks demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves improved ensemble-mean accuracy, probabilistic reliability, and physical consistency.

sections.heading: 3 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate OceanFlow on ocean simulation and forecasting tasks in terms of ensemble-mean accuracy, probabilistic reliability, ocean-specific diagnostics, physical consistency, and model complexity.

sections.heading: 3.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: ❶ Dataset We evaluate OceanFlow on GLORYS12 reanalysis with 93 ocean variables: salinity, temperature, and two velocity components at 23 depths, plus sea surface height. Four ERA5 forcing variables at two consecutive time steps provide eight atmospheric input channels. Data are processed at daily temporal and 1° spatial resolution, using daily-mean ocean states and forcings sampled at 12:00 UTC. We use 1993–2017 for training, 2018–2019 for validation, and 2020 for testing, with additional generalization tests on 2024 data. Further data details refer to the Appendix. ❷ Evaluation Metrics We evaluate ensemble-mean skill with RMSE and ACC, and probabilistic quality with empirical ensemble CRPS, spread–skill ratio (SSR), rank histograms, and coverage calibration curves. RankDev and CalibErr quantify deviations from rank uniformity and nominal coverage, respectively. Metric definitions appear in Appendix C . ❸ Baselines We compare OceanFlow with a diverse set of baselines: the general spatiotemporal model SimVP ( Tan et al., 2025a ) ; Earth-system architectures GraphCast ( Lam et al., 2023 ) and CirT ( Liu et al., 2025 ) ; and ocean-specific models WenHai ( Cui et al., 2025 ) , NeuralOM ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and DSLCast ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . We retrain SimVP, GraphCast, and CirT under the same protocol and use official pretrained weights for WenHai, NeuralOM, and DSLCast.

Table 1 reports ocean simulation results over 20 initial conditions (ICs) under prescribed atmospheric forcing, separating ocean-state uncertainty from atmospheric forecasting error. OceanFlow achieves the lowest ensemble-mean RMSE and highest ACC, together with the lowest CRPS, across all lead times. Although Perlin perturbations improve ensemble-mean RMSE over the corresponding deterministic trajectories, substantial gaps in ACC and CRPS remain relative to OceanFlow , particularly at longer lead times. This suggests that perturbation-induced spread alone may not adequately represent the state-dependent uncertainty of ocean dynamics. These results support the central premise of coherent flow matching: jointly refining the conditional residual distribution improves probabilistic quality while preserving an accurate ensemble center. Figure 4 shows that the gains extend across important sea-surface variables throughout the simulation range. The 120-day fields in Figure 3 provide a complementary spatial comparison: the ensemble mean of OceanFlow remains sharp and spatially organized, while several baselines lose fine-scale structure or exhibit pronounced spatial distortions. Figure 5 and Table 2 further assess ensemble reliability. OceanFlow yields rank distributions closer to uniform and empirical coverage closer to nominal levels, with the lowest RankDev and CalibErr at all simulation horizons.

sections.heading: 3.5 Analysis of Physical Consistency
sections.text: Figure 8: Physical diagnostics of the generated ensemble members and ensemble mean. Aggregate scores alone do not fully reveal whether the generated ensemble members are physically plausible. Moreover, in a well-formed ensemble system, the ensemble mean should not be interpreted as a single realized ocean state: as lead time increases, averaging over plausible but phase-shifted members can naturally smooth unpredictable high-wavenumber components ( Leith, 1974 ) . We therefore separate ensemble-mean structure from member-level realism in Figure 7 . For readability, we visualize representative surface variables covering typical near-surface dynamical and thermodynamic ocean processes. Solid lines show spectra of the ensemble mean, while dashed lines show member-averaged spectra computed by first evaluating each of the 20 ensemble members separately and then averaging their spectra over members and 20 ICs. The member-averaged spectra of OceanFlow are overall closer to the ground truth across these variables, indicating that individual ensemble members preserve realistic multiscale ocean variability. Meanwhile, the ensemble-mean spectra show larger deviations from the ground truth at high wavenumbers. This behavior is consistent with a well-calibrated ensemble, whose mean averages out unpredictable spectral components rather than reproducing the full spectrum of a single realization. In addition to the spectral comparison, Figure 8 reports three targeted physical diagnostics at the 120-day simulation horizon, covering SSTa mean tendency consistency, SSH-current multivariate consistency, and member-level spatial variability. OceanFlow achieves the lowest error on all three diagnostics, further indicating that it better preserves large-scale thermal evolution, dynamical SSH-current relationships, and realistic spatial variability of individual ensemble members.

sections.heading: 3.6 Ablation Study
sections.text: To validate the architectural design of OceanFlow , we conduct ablation studies through 90-day simulations over 10 ICs, as reported in Table 7 . All variants are trained same as the main method. The deterministic variants are compared against FDO: (1) w/o Factorized Dynamics replaces the factorized dynamics block with a plain convolutional block, substantially degrading simulation skill. (2) w/o State Response removes the state-conditioned response, leading to poorer accuracy and highlighting its contribution to the factorized transition. (3) w/o Adaptive State Response substitutes a fixed persistence addition for the learned response, partially recovering performance but remaining inferior to FDO. This supports adapting the state response rather than prescribing a fixed additive connection. The probabilistic comparisons further isolate the role of coherent residual transport: (4) FDO+Perlin uses the same deterministic backbone with prescribed perturbations but yields poorer probabilistic scores than OceanFlow , showing that the gains cannot be attributed to the backbone alone. (5) w/o mean correction/re-centering degrades both ensemble-mean accuracy and reliability, supporting explicit control of the predictive center. (6) w/o learned pathwise flow also reduces probabilistic performance, demonstrating the benefit of learned residual transport beyond the perturbation reference. Together, these results support the complementary roles of FDO, mean anchoring, and coherent residual transport in producing accurate and reliable ocean ensembles.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: We present OceanFlow , a coherent flow matching framework for probabilistic ocean modeling. By coupling member residuals through the evolving ensemble context, OceanFlow learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law that refines ensemble diversity around a controlled mean anchor. FDO parameterizes both the mean anchor and residual-flow velocity through a unified composition of factorized dynamics and learned state-conditioned response. Experiments demonstrate improved ensemble-mean accuracy, probabilistic reliability, and physical-consistency diagnostics, supporting coherent flow matching as an effective approach to ocean uncertainty modeling. Current ocean forecasting relies on the forcings produced by external model, extending the framework to end-to-end probabilistic ocean-atmosphere coupling may further improve ocean forecasting accuracy.

sections.heading: Deterministic ocean modeling.
sections.text: Numerical circulation models such as HYCOM ( Chassignet et al., 2007 ) and NEMO ( Madec and others, 2015 ) , together with state-estimation and reanalysis systems such as ECCO ( Forget et al., 2015 ) and Copernicus global ocean products ( Lellouche et al., 2018 ) , provide the physical and observational foundations of ocean prediction. However, the integration remains computationally intensive, limiting the practical scale of ensemble generation. Data-driven models offer efficient alternatives with increasingly competitive deterministic skill. AI-GOMS ( Xiong et al., 2023 ) develops a reusable ocean modeling backbone; XiHe ( Wang et al., 2024 ) and WenHai ( Cui et al., 2025 ) demonstrate eddy-resolving global prediction; LangYa ( Yang et al., 2024 ) addresses cross-spatiotemporal prediction. NeuralOM ( Gao et al., 2026 ) extends data-driven ocean modeling to subseasonal-to-seasonal simulation. The growing diversity of these models calls for consistent protocols to assess their relative performance. OceanForecastBench ( Jia et al., 2025 ) further supports systematic evaluation. These advances make ensemble generation more accessible, but accurate deterministic trajectories alone do not characterize the conditional uncertainty of future ocean states.

sections.heading: Probabilistic Earth-system modeling.
sections.text: Data-driven probabilistic models have found increasing application in Earth-system prediction, particularly in weather and precipitation forecasting ( Larsson et al., 2025 ; Nai et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2024 ) . Examples include MetNet ( Sønderby et al., 2020 ) , generative radar nowcasting ( Ravuri et al., 2021 ) , diffusion-based weather ensembles with GenCast ( Price et al., 2023 ) , and learned ensemble generation with FuXi-ENS ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advances, data-driven probabilistic ocean modeling remains comparatively underexplored. Conventional ocean ensembles ( Lorenz, 2017 ; Leith, 1974 ; Al Sukhni et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) represent uncertainty through initial-condition perturbations ( Toth and Kalnay, 1993 ; Molteni et al., 1996 ) , ensemble data assimilation ( Evensen, 1994 ; Houtekamer and Mitchell, 1998 ) , or multiple models ( Buizza et al., 2005 ; Palmer, 2019 ) , but require computationally expensive numerical integrations. Perturbing pretrained AI ocean models enables efficient ensemble generation and can improve ensemble-mean accuracy. However, independent rollouts lack joint distributional optimization and may misrepresent uncertainty in ocean dynamics. FuXi-ONS ( Huang et al., 2026 ) learns state-dependent, spatially structured perturbations, but its memberwise objective leaves calibration implicit and its updates do not explicitly use ensemble context. In contrast, OceanFlow learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law that couples member residuals through the evolving ensemble context, jointly refining their conditional distribution while preserving a controlled mean anchor.

sections.heading: D.1 Dataset
sections.text: We conduct the experiments on GLORYS12 reanalysis data, which provides daily mean ocean variables covering latitudes between − 80 ∘ -80^{\circ} and 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} from 1993 to the present. The data can be downloaded from https://data.marine.copernicus.eu . We use 1993–2017 for training, 2018–2019 for validation, and 2020 for the main test set. The additional 2024 evaluation in Table 4 assesses generalization beyond this test year without changing the training split. The ocean variables used in our experiments include four depth-dependent variables and one surface variable. The four depth-dependent variables are Sea salinity (S), Sea stream zonal velocity (U), Sea stream meridional velocity (V), and Sea temperature (T), each of which contains 23 depth levels. sections.heading: D.2 Data Preprocessing
sections.text: Different ocean variables and forcing variables have different physical meanings, units, and numerical ranges. To reduce the influence of these scale differences, we normalize each variable before feeding it into the model. This preprocessing step enables the model to focus more on learning the spatiotemporal evolution of ocean states rather than adapting to the magnitude discrepancies among variables. We first compute daily climatological means for ocean salinity, temperature, and sea-surface height using the first 365 days of each year in the 1993–2017 training period. The resulting climatology has dimensions 365 × 47 × 181 × 360 365\times 47\times 181\times 360 , corresponding to days, variables, latitude, and longitude, respectively. The 47 variables comprise salinity and temperature at 23 depth levels each, together with sea-surface height. These variables are converted into anomalies by subtracting their corresponding daily climatological means. We then compute variable-wise means and standard deviations over the same training period, using anomaly fields for these 47 variables and the original fields for the remaining variables, and apply these statistics for normalization. For forcing variables, means and standard deviations are computed from ERA5 data over 1959–2017. Each variable is normalized independently using its own mean and standard deviation. Specifically, for each variable, we first subtract its corresponding mean and then divide the result by its corresponding standard deviation. For land regions, the original ocean variables contain ‘nan’ values. Before inputting the data into the model, these missing values are filled with zeros after normalization. The Land-sea mask is used as a static variable to indicate the distribution of land and ocean regions.

sections.heading: E.5 Inference
sections.text: Structured perturbations of an observed ocean state establish the initial member conditions. At each day, the deterministic reference advances these conditions, and mean correction and coherent residual transport produce the evaluated ensemble through Eqs. equation 48 and equation 8 . Reference outputs supply the next member conditions, while the shared context is reinitialized from the new condition. The coherent law therefore governs the conditional ensemble at each transition, with the reference determining progression in physical time. All reported OceanFlow ensemble metrics evaluate the transformed ensemble rather than the raw reference. Simulation takes ( 𝐅 t , 𝐅 t + 1 ) (\mathbf{F}_{t},\mathbf{F}_{t+1}) from the test reanalysis, whereas prediction uses OneForecast atmospheric states. OneForecast is initialized at the 12:00 UTC state aligned with the ocean IC and advanced through four 6-hour steps per ocean day, supplying the current-day and next-day forcing pair. The ocean rollout protocol otherwise remains unchanged. The preliminary coupled-forcing experiment in Table 5 instead takes atmospheric states from an independently running two-way PnP-Corrector system. Here “two-way” identifies the forcing source: OceanFlow does not feed its ensemble back into that atmospheric model, and end-to-end probabilistic ocean–atmosphere coupling remains future work.

Affiliation: Tsinghua University Fan Xu Hao Wu Xiaomeng Huang Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Abstract Probabilistic ocean modeling is essential for risk-aware marine operations, climate analysis, and scientific decision-making, where downstream decisions depend on the conditional distribution of future ocean states rather than a single deterministic trajectory. Recent data-driven ocean models have made deterministic global ocean modeling increasingly accurate and efficient, but probabilistic ocean modeling remains underdeveloped. Specifically, perturbation-driven ensembles can create spread without explicitly optimizing the joint distribution of their members, often yielding poor calibration and physical inconsistency. To address these issues, we propose OceanFlow , a coherent flow matching framework for probabilistic global ocean modeling. OceanFlow first establishes a sharp, stable mean anchor for the conditional ensemble. Flow matching then learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law that jointly reshapes the residual distribution around this anchor at each transition, preserving the predictive center while refining state-dependent uncertainty. We further introduce a Factorized Dynamics Operator (FDO), which combines factorized transitions with a learned state-conditioned response to parameterize the mean anchor and residual-flow velocity. Extensive experiments show that OceanFlow improves ensemble-mean accuracy, probabilistic reliability, and physical-consistency diagnostics over competitive baselines, supporting coherent flow matching as an effective route toward data-driven probabilistic ocean modeling. Code is available at https://github.com/YuanGao-YG/OceanFlow . 1 Introduction Ocean modeling is essential for risk-aware marine operations, climate analysis, and scientific decision-making ( Kalnay, 2003 ; Lellouche et al., 2018 ; Tan et al., 2025b ) . Incomplete observations leave uncertainty in the initial ocean state, while nonlinear dynamics can amplify small state errors into substantially different future evolutions ( Lorenz, 2017 ; Leith, 1974 ) . Even an accurate deterministic estimate cannot characterize the range of plausible outcomes or their relative likelihoods. Probabilistic modeling can address this limitation by representing the conditional distribution of future ocean states, providing uncertainty information beyond a single trajectory. Recent data-driven models, including AI-GOMS ( Xiong et al., 2023 ) , XiHe ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , LangYa ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , and WenHai ( Cui et al., 2025 ) , have substantially advanced deterministic global ocean modeling, combining competitive predictive accuracy with considerably faster inference than traditional numerical models. These gains make ocean modeling more affordable and provide a strong foundation for efficient ensemble generation. However, despite this progress in deterministic modeling, data-driven probabilistic ocean modeling remains comparatively underexplored. Similar to initial-condition perturbation in numerical ensemble forecasting, data-driven ocean models can be extended to probabilistic modeling by perturbing their initial states and evolving the resulting members with a pretrained deterministic model ( Hao et al., 2025 ) . Prescribed perturbations can generate ensemble spread and improve ensemble-mean accuracy through averaging. However, members evolve independently without joint distributional optimization, potentially yielding distributions that deviate from physically plausible ocean variability and fail to faithfully represent uncertainty in the underlying dynamics. FuXi-ONS ( Huang et al., 2026 ) advances beyond prescribed noise by learning state-dependent, spatially structured perturbations for autoregressive ocean prediction. This provides a more adaptive representation of ensemble variability. Nevertheless, its memberwise prediction objective leaves ensemble calibration implicit, while member updates do not explicitly account for the evolving ensemble context. These advances motivate a central question: how can the ensemble be jointly refined to more faithfully characterize uncertainty in the underlying ocean dynamics while maintaining a controlled predictive center? Figure 1: Learning coherent ensemble laws for ocean modeling. (a) Deterministic modeling produces a single trajectory. (b) OceanFlow represents ocean uncertainty through a mean-anchored ensemble, jointly refining member residuals under a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law at each transition. To answer this question, we propose OceanFlow , a coherent flow matching framework for probabilistic ocean modeling. As illustrated in Figure 1 , OceanFlow learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law for the residual ensemble around a controlled mean anchor at each transition. This law couples member-specific transport paths through a shared velocity field conditioned on the ocean state and evolving ensemble context. Ensemble diversity is thus jointly refined as a conditional residual distribution, with final recentering preserving the predictive center. We further introduce a Factorized Dynamics Operator (FDO) that parameterizes both the mean anchor and residual-flow velocity through a unified composition of factorized dynamics and learned state-conditioned response. Our contributions can be summarized as: • We propose OceanFlow , a coherent flow matching framework for probabilistic ocean modeling that learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law around the mean anchor center. By coupling member residuals through the evolving ensemble context, it jointly refines the conditional distribution while preserving a controlled mean anchor. • We introduce a Factorized Dynamics Operator (FDO), which unifies factorized dynamics and a learned state-conditioned response within a single conditional operator formulation. FDO supports both an accurate deterministic reference for the mean anchor and a structured velocity field for residual transport. • Extensive experiments on global ocean simulation and forecasting tasks demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves improved ensemble-mean accuracy, probabilistic reliability, and physical consistency. 2 Method 2.1 Problem Formulation Let 𝐎 t ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{O}_{t}\in\mathcal{X} denote the ocean state and 𝐅 t , 𝐅 t + 1 \mathbf{F}_{t},\mathbf{F}_{t+1} the external forcing. Aggregate scores alone do not fully reveal whether the generated ensemble members are physically plausible. Moreover, in a well-formed ensemble system, the ensemble mean should not be interpreted as a single realized ocean state: as lead time increases, averaging over plausible but phase-shifted members can naturally smooth unpredictable high-wavenumber components ( Leith, 1974 ) . We therefore separate ensemble-mean structure from member-level realism in Figure 7 . For readability, we visualize representative surface variables covering typical near-surface dynamical and thermodynamic ocean processes. Solid lines show spectra of the ensemble mean, while dashed lines show member-averaged spectra computed by first evaluating each of the 20 ensemble members separately and then averaging their spectra over members and 20 ICs. The member-averaged spectra of OceanFlow are overall closer to the ground truth across these variables, indicating that individual ensemble members preserve realistic multiscale ocean variability. Meanwhile, the ensemble-mean spectra show larger deviations from the ground truth at high wavenumbers. This behavior is consistent with a well-calibrated ensemble, whose mean averages out unpredictable spectral components rather than reproducing the full spectrum of a single realization. In addition to the spectral comparison, Figure 8 reports three targeted physical diagnostics at the 120-day simulation horizon, covering SSTa mean tendency consistency, SSH-current multivariate consistency, and member-level spatial variability. OceanFlow achieves the lowest error on all three diagnostics, further indicating that it better preserves large-scale thermal evolution, dynamical SSH-current relationships, and realistic spatial variability of individual ensemble members. 3.6 Ablation Study To validate the architectural design of OceanFlow , we conduct ablation studies through 90-day simulations over 10 ICs, as reported in Table 7 . All variants are trained same as the main method. The deterministic variants are compared against FDO: (1) w/o Factorized Dynamics replaces the factorized dynamics block with a plain convolutional block, substantially degrading simulation skill. (2) w/o State Response removes the state-conditioned response, leading to poorer accuracy and highlighting its contribution to the factorized transition. (3) w/o Adaptive State Response substitutes a fixed persistence addition for the learned response, partially recovering performance but remaining inferior to FDO. This supports adapting the state response rather than prescribing a fixed additive connection. The probabilistic comparisons further isolate the role of coherent residual transport: (4) FDO+Perlin uses the same deterministic backbone with prescribed perturbations but yields poorer probabilistic scores than OceanFlow , showing that the gains cannot be attributed to the backbone alone. (5) w/o mean correction/re-centering degrades both ensemble-mean accuracy and reliability, supporting explicit control of the predictive center. (6) w/o learned pathwise flow also reduces probabilistic performance, demonstrating the benefit of learned residual transport beyond the perturbation reference. Together, these results support the complementary roles of FDO, mean anchoring, and coherent residual transport in producing accurate and reliable ocean ensembles. 3.7 Training Protocol and Efficiency Analysis Table 6: Parameter comparison for retrained models. By coupling member residuals through the evolving ensemble context, OceanFlow learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law that refines ensemble diversity around a controlled mean anchor. FDO parameterizes both the mean anchor and residual-flow velocity through a unified composition of factorized dynamics and learned state-conditioned response. Experiments demonstrate improved ensemble-mean accuracy, probabilistic reliability, and physical-consistency diagnostics, supporting coherent flow matching as an effective approach to ocean uncertainty modeling. Current ocean forecasting relies on the forcings produced by external model, extending the framework to end-to-end probabilistic ocean-atmosphere coupling may further improve ocean forecasting accuracy.
